The CMSX-2 superalloy used in this study had a chemical composition with the main alloying elements being Cr (8.0 wt%), W (8.0 wt%), Ta (6.0 wt%), Al (5.6 wt%), and Co (4.6 wt%).
The initial microstructure of the CMSX-2 superalloy was dominated by cuboidal, ordered gamma prime (γ') precipitates with a volume fraction of about 75% and an average size of 0.5 μm.

Hydrogen was introduced into the CMSX-2 samples by two methods: 1) cathodic potentiostatic charging in a molten salt mixture at 150°C for 5 hours, and 2) high-pressure (138 MPa), high-temperature (300°C) gas phase charging for 15 days.
High-pressure, high-temperature hydrogen charging resulted in a uniform hydrogen concentration of ~5000 appm throughout the CMSX-2 samples.
Hydrogen charging, especially the high-pressure, high-temperature method, significantly increased work hardening and reduced the true uniform elongation to almost zero in tensile testing.
Hydrogen charging dramatically reduced the number of cycles to failure by up to two orders of magnitude in fatigue testing of CMSX-2.

The most significant hydrogen-induced microstructural changes were enhanced dislocation accumulation in the gamma (γ) matrix and more extensive cross-slip of superdislocations in the gamma prime (γ') precipitates.
Hydrogen-charged CMSX-2 samples exhibited a much more brittle fracture appearance, with a planar fracture surface oriented normal to the tensile axis.
Microscopic observations suggested that hydrogen-enhanced strain localization and premature plastic failure in the gamma (γ) phase led to the observed embrittlement in hydrogen-charged CMSX-2.

The high-pressure, high-temperature hydrogen charging method resulted in more dramatic changes in the mechanical properties of CMSX-2 compared to the localized hydrogen introduced by molten salt charging.

The CMSX-2 superalloy is important for applications such as advanced earth-to-orbit propulsion technology, where understanding the role of hydrogen is crucial.
Cathodic potentiostatic charging in a molten salt mixture at 150°C for 5 hours was used as one method to introduce hydrogen into the CMSX-2 samples.
High-pressure (138 MPa), high-temperature (300°C) gas phase charging for 15 days was the other method used to introduce a uniform hydrogen concentration of ~5000 appm throughout the CMSX-2 samples.

The enhanced dislocation accumulation in the gamma (γ) matrix and more extensive cross-slip of superdislocations in the gamma prime (γ') precipitates contributed to the increased work hardening and reduced uniform elongation observed in hydrogen-charged CMSX-2.
